extracted.intended_audience: employee benefit plan sponsors, plan administrators, and ERISA/benefits counsel
extracted.subtask_description: High-level FAQs explaining how the Supreme Court’s Loper Bright decision changes judicial review of agency regulations and what plan sponsors should do about compliance, litigation risk, and agency rulemaking affecting employee benefit plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of judicial review after Loper Bright
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts must exercise independent judgment when determining the best interpretation of a statute and cannot simply defer to agency interpretations, even when the statute is silent or ambiguous and the agency interpretation is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change will likely increase courts’ scrutiny of federal agency regulations that are subject to legal challenges. Courts may still treat agency interpretations as persuasive in appropriate circumstances, particularly on technical matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: When agency interpretations remain persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may still view agency interpretations as persuasive, particularly with respect to their expertise on technical issues, and more so when the agency’s interpretation was adopted soon after a law’s enactment and has remained consistent over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and early adoption of an interpretation tend to increase its persuasive weight; courts are more likely to defer to longstanding agency views even under independent-review regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standard where Congress expressly delegates authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A different standard of review applies when Congress expressly delegates authority to a federal agency to promulgate regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will apply a narrower scope of review in these cases, including assessing (1) the delegation’s constitutionality, (2) whether the agency acted within the scope of the delegation, and (3) whether the agency followed a reasoned process when issuing the regulations. This narrower scope suggests legal challenges to regulations issued under express delegation may be less likely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright doesn’t invalidate or eliminate any existing regulations, including those applicable to employee benefit plans; the ruling also specifically preserves earlier court decisions upholding agency regulations based on the application of Chevron deference, at least for now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although existing regulations remain in force, subsequent court decisions (and related decisions like Corner Post) may open new avenues to challenge longstanding rules depending on when a party is 'affected' by a regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of APA statute of limitations (Corner Post implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act’s six-year statute of limitations for challenging a regulation doesn’t start when a regulation is published, but instead when the person or entity bringing the legal challenge was first affected by the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person or entity newly subject to an existing regulation may be able to bring a timely challenge even if the rule was promulgated years earlier; this may invite challenges to longstanding employee benefits regulations by newly affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to continue complying with existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan sponsors and plans should continue to comply with existing agency final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Loper Bright didn’t eliminate regulations, sponsors should maintain compliance but also monitor employee benefits litigation that may change compliance obligations over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty for reliance on regulatory safe harbors
rubrics_metrics.description: There is speculation about whether complying with regulatory safe harbors will continue to provide the protection it has in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of safe harbors include DOL’s 404(c) and QDIA fiduciary relief and the ERISA exemption for voluntary plans. Sponsors with concerns should consult legal counsel about the implications for specific regulations or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate action required by plan sponsors
rubrics_metrics.description: No, plan sponsors don’t need to take any immediate action; it’s business as usual for day-to-day plan administration and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsors should continue to monitor and analyze new agency guidance, consider discussing with counsel and industry trade groups whether to submit comments on proposed regulations, and monitor litigation challenging new or existing employee benefits regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term health and welfare regulations likely affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright is likely to affect several recent and soon-to-be issued regulations impacting group health plans, including the final ACA section 1557 nondiscrimination regulation, the final MHPAEA nonquantitative treatment limitations regulation, regulations addressing covered prescription drugs as essential health benefits for self-funded and large insured group health plans, and rules on accumulating manufacturer financial assistance toward participant cost-sharing limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of these rules are already being challenged in court; Loper Bright may make it easier for challengers to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term retirement regulations likely affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright is likely to influence lawsuits challenging recent DOL regulations affecting retirement plans, such as DOL’s 2022 ESG investing rule and the DOL regulation expanding the scope of fiduciary investment advice under ERISA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts have temporarily blocked implementation citing Loper Bright, and pending appeals may require lower courts to reconsider prior Chevron-based decisions. By contrast, SECURE 2.0 implementation appears less likely to be delayed where statutes expressly authorize agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express delegation can protect implementation of statutory programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many SECURE 2.0 provisions direct or expressly authorize agencies to issue implementing regulations or guidance, and where Congress expressly delegates authority, agencies’ implementing actions are less vulnerable to Loper Bright-style attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOL and IRS have already released proposed regulations and subregulatory guidance for SECURE 2.0 provisions; because of express delegation, these actions so far have not generated legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on agencies' choice between formal rulemaking and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may decide the extra effort and prolonged timeframe involved in public notice-and-comment rulemaking isn’t justified if courts no longer defer to reasonable agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This could lead agencies to issue fewer formal regulations and more subregulatory guidance as a policy choice to avoid exposure to increased judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on subregulatory guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies frequently issue guidance in forms other than regulations (revenue rulings, notices, FAQs, bulletins, technical releases, fact sheets, administrative manuals, form instructions, self-compliance tools), and such guidance rarely received Chevron deference, so Loper Bright should have little direct impact on how courts handle challenges to subregulatory guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subregulatory guidance historically has not benefitted from Chevron deference, agencies may rely more on these tools even if courts scrutinize formal regulations more closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of increased litigation challenging regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright may embolden plaintiffs and lead to more litigation challenging new (and possibly long-standing) final regulations now that courts will not simply defer to agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even before Loper Bright, litigation challenging perceived partisan regulations was common; plaintiffs may forum-shop for favorable courts, and preliminary rulings may vary until courts establish new precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible legislative and congressional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may respond by writing more detailed legislation, mandating congressional approval of major agency regulations, increasing congressional staff to draft legislation, creating a new regulatory agency, or legislatively resurrecting the Chevron standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These responses would be controversial and likely take years to evolve; in the short term, Loper Bright could spur more active dialogue between Congress and the executive branch over interpretation and implementation of law.
